questions.q: What does it mean for an index to 'cover' a query?
options: Every column the query references anywhere — SELECT list, WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY — is available directly from the index, as a key or included column
The index has been rebuilt within the last 24 hours
The index is the clustered index for that table
The query uses a table hint to force that index
questions.explain: A covering index supplies every referenced column itself, so SQL Server never needs to visit the clustered index to fetch anything else.

questions.q: What does a covering index's plan look like compared to a non-covering one, per this lesson?
options: A single Index Seek, with no Key Lookup or Nested Loops join needed
It always requires two Index Scans instead of one
It's identical in every respect to the non-covering plan
It always forces a Clustered Index Scan
questions.explain: The non-covering plan pairs an Index Seek with a per-row Key Lookup joined via Nested Loops; the covering plan collapses that down to a single Index Seek.

questions.q: In the example, which change made the index on Orders(CustomerId) covering for a query selecting OrderId, OrderDate, and TotalDue?
options: Adding INCLUDE (OrderDate, TotalDue) to the index definition
Rebuilding the index with FILLFACTOR = 100
Adding a WHERE clause to the index
Converting the index to a clustered index
questions.explain: Adding OrderDate and TotalDue as included columns makes every column the query needs available directly from the nonclustered index.

questions.q: What is the real cost of making an index covering, per this lesson?
options: A wider index means more disk space and more write cost on every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE that touches it
Covering indexes have no downside at all
Covering indexes can only be created on heaps
Covering indexes disable the query optimizer's cost-based decisions entirely
questions.explain: Every additional key or included column widens the index's leaf pages, increasing storage and the maintenance cost on every write.

questions.q: Given a storage budget that can only widen one index, which query should you prioritize covering, per this lesson's guidance?
options: The dashboard query that runs every five seconds, not the report that runs once a month
Whichever query was written most recently
The report query, because reports are always more important
Neither — covering indexes should never be prioritized by query frequency
questions.explain: The lesson's guidance is query-driven: cover the queries that run constantly and matter for performance, since a rarely run query's savings are rarely collected.
